Subjective comfort showed consistent seat-height and seat-height × stage effects across the primary and sensitivity analyses. An exploratory CRITIC integration using a within-muscle-standardized log-RMS sEMG summary placed H2 (80% of popliteal height) first among the four tested conditions; the leading position of H2 was retained across alternative sEMG scaling approaches and when the sEMG component was excluded or its orientation reversed, although H2 and H4 nearly tied under the reversed orientation. Overall, seat-height effects varied across task stages and outcome domains. H2 emerged as the highest-scoring tested condition under the present protocol, providing a task-specific basis for future validation.

Abstract Background Segment Anything Model (SAM), a prompt‐guided foundation model, exhibits substantial potential for medical image segmentation by incorporating prior knowledge through user‐defined prompts. However, the application of SAM in radiotherapy target delineation remains limited. Purpose This study proposes a feasible prompt‐guided interactive delineation workflow driven by an optimized SAM. Methods A total of 100 rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy cases were collected (60 for training and 40 for testing). This study utilized bounding‐box prompts to guide SAM for GTV segmentation. Physicians manually draw box prompts on certain slices, while box prompts for the remaining slices are automatically generated using an interpolation strategy. Four fine‐tuning strategies for SAM training were evaluated, and the impact of prompt numbers and placements was assessed as well. The performance of the finalized workflow with optimized SAM was compared with five state‐of‐the‐art (SOTA) models, and its robustness to prompt variations in middle‐slice selection and box‐prompt margins was analyzed. Results Compared to other fine‐tuning methods, freezing the image encoder obtained the most stable performance. Prompts on only 3 slices achieved accuracy comparable to prompts on all slices. The placement of the middle‐slice prompt exhibited negligible impact ( p > 0.05). The finalized SAM‐driven workflow outperformed end‐to‐end baseline models both visually and quantitatively (3D DSC: 0.92 vs 0.80; 3D HD95: 2.73 vs 12.70; IoU: 0.86 vs 0.67; Sensitivity: 91.20% vs 85.98%; Precision: 93.65% vs 79.23%), while maintaining stable performance across certain prompt variations. Conclusions The proposed SAM‐driven interactive workflow with as few as 3 box prompts achieves favorable accuracy of GTV segmentation for rectal cancer neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Fertilizer advisory systems built on machine learning must issue a recommendation for every field, yet soil-test sampling gaps mean that many fields arrive with covariates that are only partially observed. The framework treats abstention as a first-class output, defines the abstention-risk profile as the conditional over-application rate among retained cases, and proves that under a bounded calibration gap the profile is controlled by the abstention threshold and the sampling-gap severity. A design-based evaluation is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 52 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The bound converts an evaluation target into an auditable abstention rule, and the paper argues that advisory evaluations should report abstention-risk profiles alongside aggregate accuracy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Phenological stage labels collected from ground observations are unevenly distributed across space and time, and the resulting temporal label noise propagates into any downstream yield inference that treats those labels as ground truth. the present analysis formalises the problem as a semi-supervised alignment task in which a small set of stage-labelled observations must be reconciled with a larger pool of unlabelled or weakly labelled crop sequences, and it evaluates the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) estimator under a declared variance structure. No observational data are used or claimed: the analysis is a replication-based design evaluation in which the between-cluster standard deviation was set to 6.0, the residual standard deviation to 4.5, and the intraclass correlation to 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis found that 54 clusters were required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power under this variance structure, and that power curves, minimum detectable effect curves, coefficient intervals, residual diagnostics and kernel density estimates of estimated power all behaved in the manner the design theory predicts. The contribution is a formal statement of the temporal-label-noise problem, a semi-supervised alignment operator with stated consistency conditions, and a design-level characterisation of how much ground observation is needed before BACI inference on phenological alignment becomes reliable. The implication is that temporal label noise is not a nuisance to be cleaned post hoc but a design parameter that governs the cluster budget of any yield inference pipeline.

Ransomware remains a critical threat to modern enterprise and personal computing infrastructure.Traditional signature-based detection mechanisms exhibit operational degradation when confronted with previously unobserved polymorphic or zero-day variants.This paper presents SentinelML, an autonomous endpoint detection architecture that identifies ransomware activity through 19 dynamic behavioral indicators collected entirely in user space without requiring kernel-level filter drivers.By sampling filesystem Shannon entropy, process concurrency anomalies, shadow copy deletion commands, and cryptographic module bindings, SentinelML trains a local Random Forest classifier that operates as an unprivileged host daemon.To address operational triage transparency, the local classifier is coupled with an architecturally decoupled Large Language Model (LLM) advisory explainer operating via an isolated HTTPS interface.We conduct an exhaustive technical audit of the production system: confirming that Shannon entropy accounts for 41.31% of aggregate Gini importance, documenting the operational tradeoffs of heuristic user-space proxies, analyzing platform asymmetry between Windows and Linux deployments, and evaluating the system strictly as an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).Finally, we disclose that previously reported internal metrics (0.9567 accuracy across candidate algorithms) could not be independently reproduced due to unpreserved training artifacts, and establish an open empirical evaluation protocol for reproducible validation.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the learning and developmental contexts in which young children grow, learn, and interact. Guided by an ecological perspective, this systematic conceptual mapping review examines 86 resources to explore what young children should learn and how they should be taught. Four themes were identified through thematic analysis: (1) holistic competencies for young children, encompassing foundational cognitive and social–emotional skills, physical and mental well-being, executive functions, learning dispositions, and AI literacy; (2) governance for AI integration in early childhood education; (3) professional development and systemic support for educators; and (4) play-based learning and human-centered approaches in AI-enhanced contexts. The findings suggest that thriving in the AI age requires moving beyond isolated digital skills toward holistic development, supported by a cohesive infrastructure that links classroom practice with structural governance. These findings highlight the necessity of cultivating holistic competencies beyond basic AI literacy in curriculum design, preparing children to navigate an ever-changing digital world. Furthermore, they underscore the imperative for robust institutional support, particularly through participatory research to support age-appropriate pedagogy and educators’ digital confidence, while highlighting the value of playful early learning. Concurrently, these insights establish a theoretical framework for future empirical research, offer actionable strategies for ethical child-centred AI implementation, and provide strategic directions for policy and practice to address the critical demand for transformative knowledge in early childhood education.

Nurses working rotating shifts face structural constraints on their use of preventive dental services that are not captured by conventional access models. The framework specifies how shift rotation compresses the discretionary time available for scheduling and attending appointments, how circadian disruption raises the perceived cost of non-urgent care, and how the fixed-effects design isolates within-nurse variation in attendance behaviour across shift cycles. The analysis is framed as a proposed empirical strategy rather than a completed study: no primary data were collected for the present analysis. The contribution is a mechanism-centred account that distinguishes occupational time poverty from income poverty, geographic access barriers and health literacy deficits, and that specifies the conditions under which shift-schedule effects on dental hygiene attendance should be identifiable. Dental hygiene appointment non-attendance among Nigerian hospital nurses is best understood as a scheduling-constraint phenomenon with a circadian component, and that interventions targeting reminder systems or oral health education without addressing shift structure are likely to produce attenuated effects. The framework has implications for how hospital occupational health services and dental hygiene clinics coordinate appointment availability.

User-facing LLM agents must identify which behavioral policies apply at each turn, but evaluating every policy with an LLM is costly. We introduce Signals and Queries (S&Q), a lightweight first-stage relevance filter developed for Parlant 4.0 that removes at least 30% of candidate policies before downstream evaluation while preserving high recall. For each policy, an LLM generates activating examples and hard negatives offline. An independent logistic classifier trained on their embeddings then predicts relevance using embeddings and vector dot products, with no per-turn LLM calls. This shifts expensive relevance evaluation to a smaller candidate set, while allowing each policy's classifier to be updated independently. Evaluated against 9,144 LLM-judge relevance labels covering 254 $τ^2$-bench conversation prefixes and 36 airline policies, S&Q achieves higher precision than top-K and cosine-threshold retrieval at every evaluated recall level, with consistent results across two embedding providers. These findings support inexpensive, per-policy classification as a practical first stage for reducing downstream evaluation workload in customer-facing agents.

Abstract Evaluation of AI-generated patient communication lacks standardized frameworks, and automated metrics may not reflect clinical utility. We leveraged a staged rollout of GPT-generated draft responses (GDRs) to patient portal messages. Thirty primary care physicians received drafts from September 2023 to August 2024 under two conditions: an intervention group where AI drafts were displayed and edited ( n = 21,073), and a non-displayed group where drafts were generated but never shown to physicians, who composed responses independently ( n = 45,127). We evaluated messages using BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and Flesch Reading Ease, and then correlated automated metrics with blinded physician ratings of effectiveness, misunderstanding potential, and harm. In the intervention group, 2264 (11%) drafts were incorporated into final messages with high semantic alignment (BERTScore F1 = 0.93). In the non-displayed group, independent physician messages showed moderate similarity to unseen drafts (BERTScore F1 = 0.83). Despite comparable semantic scores, physicians preferred human-authored messages (4.24/5). BERTScore correlated with physician quality ratings in the intervention group but not in the non-displayed. Automated metrics demonstrated context-dependent validity; they assessed editing fidelity but failed to evaluate whether AI-generated content matches independent human performance. Rigorous evaluation of clinical generative AI requires validation of metric meaning within specific use contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models increasingly address users in the register of care: they remember personal details, adopt a first-person emotional voice, and sustain relationships across many sessions. This anthropomorphic mode of interaction generates risks that output-level metrics capture poorly, because the same empathic utterance may console one user, entrap a second, and consolidate a delusion in a third. Governance has responded in two ways. Uniform restriction refuses sensitive requests or suppresses empathic phrasing across all outputs; group-targeted protection profiles vulnerable populations and applies stricter or prohibitive rules to them. This article argues that both fail. Uniform restriction mislocates harm in the lexical form of responses rather than in the trajectory of a relationship; group-based protection depends on a list that can never be complete, treats a fluid property as a static attribute of persons, and converts protective attention into stigmatizing labels. Drawing on philosophical work that treats vulnerability as universal, relational, and differentiated, we propose that the unit of ethical governance should be the vulnerability situation rather than the vulnerable group, develop a typology of five situations - physical, emotional, cognitive, autonomy, and relational - and specify seven principles into requirements that guide response calibration without diagnosing or persistently classifying users. The framework relocates AI safety from output control to relational safety.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Part of being smart is being better at getting smarter. Artificial intelligence can amplify that capacity while human judgment shapes how the tool is used. The same technology can also take over problem selection, verification, and learning, reducing the advantage that initially capable users bring to it. This paper develops that transition argument using evidence from writing, customer support, consulting, entrepreneurship, and mathematics education. A simple model shows how persistent differences in improvement rates compound. It then lets those rates change as AI does more of the work. Equal rates can stop the relative gap from widening. Closing it requires the person behind to catch up, or AI to supply so much of the capability that the remaining human differences matter little. With broad access, enough material resources, and help directed toward their own goals, people could live well with less dependence on their starting intelligence or diligence. AI could even help them become more willing to correct their mistakes. A person who keeps refusing help limits what an assistant respecting that choice may do. Meanwhile, early winners may keep their ownership and influence after everyone else gains comparable abilities. The ethical question concerns both people’s ability to live well and their say in the systems supporting them. The central issue is whether broadly available assistance catches up before temporary advantages become durable concentrations of power.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Traffic congestion is a major challenge in urban areas, particularly at road intersections where a large number of vehicles compete for limited road space. Conventional traffic signal systems generally operate using predefined time intervals, which do not always reflect the actual traffic conditions on the road. As a result, vehicles may wait unnecessarily on less congested roads while heavily congested roads continue to face long queues. To address this issue, this paper presents a Smart Traffic Signal Management System that uses artificial intelligence and computer vision techniques for real-time traffic monitoring and adaptive signal control. The proposed system uses camera-based video input to continuously observe traffic at a four-way intersection. A YOLO-based object detection model is used to identify and count vehicles from the captured video, while the detected vehicle information is analyzed to estimate the traffic density and queue level on each road. Based on the calculated traffic condition, the system dynamically determines the priority and duration of the green signal for different directions. This approach allows the signal timing to respond to changing traffic conditions instead of relying only on fixed schedules. The system also includes a monitoring interface through which authorized traffic personnel can observe vehicle counts, traffic density, signal status, and other relevant information. A manual override facility is provided to allow human intervention in situations where the automated detection system is affected by poor visibility, unusual traffic conditions, or other operational issues. The collected traffic information can be stored in a centralized database and used for generating periodic reports and analyzing traffic patterns. The proposed system was developed and tested in a controlled environment using traffic video data to evaluate its ability to detect vehicles and determine traffic density. The results demonstrate that an AI-assisted adaptive signal system can provide more responsive traffic management compared with conventional fixed-time signal operation. The system can potentially reduce unnecessary vehicle waiting time, improve the utilization of green signal periods, and provide traffic authorities with useful real-time information for intersection management.

This article examines how users cognitively process social chatbot output as a novel form of participatory, generative “character,” co-produced through human–AI interaction. Reporting on the results of empirical research on user responses to the social chatbot platform character.ai, it shows how cognitive stylistic and narratological approaches to character can be utilised but also must be developed to analyse and theorise users’ experience of and interaction with generative AI agents. It makes specific contributions to cognitive stylistics, rhetorical narratology, character studies, and research on gen AI chatbots by: (1) illustrating how the concept of mind-modelling can used to analyse the ways in which users linguistically anthropomorphise social chatbots; (2) developing two new audience response types – transmimetic and hypermimetic – to respectively capture ways in which users assess chatbots against prior knowledge of characters across media and cases where chatbots appear so convincingly human that users question their ontological status; (3) proposing the concept of ‘postdigital misperception’ to reflect the way that users of AI can misattribute the ontological origin of an LLM’s output. The article demonstrates how social chatbots are reshaping how users understand character, agency, and reality in interactive, participatory and generative digital contexts and argues that social chatbots epitomise postdigital experience in blurring the distinction between the digital and non-digital as well as fictional and real.

Autonomous mechanical weeding in computer agriculture must learn from sparse, delayed crop-injury signals, yet the safety cost of exploratory actions is borne by the crop rather than the learner. the present analysis formalises the problem as a constrained regret minimisation over a safety-constrained Markov decision process in which injury feedback arrives with a lag and the injury budget is finite. A Lagrangian safety-constrained regret bound is derived that separates the statistical cost of sparse rewards from the safety cost of delayed feedback, and the bound is evaluated through a replication-based design analysis of the before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5 percentage point effect, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the detectable effect at small cluster counts. The contribution is a safety-constrained regret formulation that makes the injury budget an explicit design parameter rather than an emergent property of reward shaping, together with a design-analysis protocol that quantifies how delayed feedback inflates the cluster requirement for evaluating such learners in the field.

Sparse soil-moisture probe networks in computer agriculture produce field estimates whose reliability is rarely characterised before deployment. The framework treats the field as a separable spatio-temporal process with a Matérn spatial covariance and an exponential temporal covariance, and it formalises interpolation as posterior mean prediction under a declared observation model. The main result is a bound on the integrated posterior variance that holds uniformly over the field and degrades gracefully as probe spacing increases. A replication-based evaluation of the ['Intercept', 'exposure', 'group', 'severity'] estimator was conducted: 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). The study characterises the behaviour of the ordinary least squares estimator under the stated process. Across 600 replications the estimated bias was -0.01564 for the intercept and 0.00012 for the exposure coefficient, with RMSE 0.86891 and 0.0156 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The bound and the estimator diagnostics together specify the conditions under which sparse-network interpolation can be trusted and the conditions under which it cannot.

Locust swarm trajectory prediction under radar surveillance gaps is a coverage problem before it is an accuracy problem: a forecaster that reports a nominal 95% interval but covers the true swarm position in only four of five cases will misdirect aerial control assets even when its point forecasts are unbiased. The estimator is a linear model of the form intercept, exposure, group and severity, fitted by ordinary least squares to 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2, seed 714928413). The evaluation characterises the sampling behaviour of the estimator that any graph ensemble's readout layer must inherit. Across the 600 replications the intercept was estimated with a bias of -0.07778 and an RMSE of 0.87843, the exposure coefficient with a bias of 0.00173 and an RMSE of 0.01625, and the nominal 95% confidence intervals achieved empirical coverage of 1.0 for both parameters. Coverage calibration, not point accuracy, is the binding constraint on operational deployment of graph-based swarm predictors, and it specifies the calibration diagnostics that a radar-gap-aware ensemble must satisfy before its intervals can be trusted for asset allocation.

documents.abstract: Introduction Digitally recorded respiratory sounds provide a practical source of physiological information for computer-assisted auscultation. Their acoustic presentation varies across subjects, recording locations, devices, filtering conditions, and environmental noise. Most classification models map acoustic representations directly to disease labels, which provides limited access to the auscultation findings associated with each prediction. This study investigated whether respiratory acoustic representations could be organized into structured evidence for classification across different label settings and evaluation levels. Methods We developed Evi-CARD to organize respiratory sound representations into structured evidence for classification. A frozen Open Respiratory Acoustic Foundation Model (OPERA) encodes overlapping 8 s segments, from which a concept-aligned pathway estimates wheeze, crackle, inspiration, and expiration together with learned evidence weights. An attention-constrained residual pathway preserves complementary acoustic information, although its attention ceiling does not strictly bound the residual pathway’s contribution to the final logits. Separate disease-query layers adapt the shared evidence representation to each classification setting. We assessed BRACETS A2 and A3 by subject-independent five-fold validation at the recording level and KAUH-primary by subject-independent five-fold validation at the patient level for Healthy vs. Obstructive classification. Each assessment was conducted within its source cohort and was not an external-validation experiment. Results On BRACETS, Evi-CARD achieved balanced accuracies of 77.8% for the A2 three-class task and 70.2% for the more granular A3 five-class task. On KAUH-primary, pooled patient-level out-of-fold evaluation yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 95.1%, a balanced accuracy of 88.0%, a Macro F1 of 88.1%, and an expected calibration error of 5.1%. Across HF_Lung_V1, SPRSound, and ICBHI, the complete concept layer also provided more accurate and better-calibrated concept predictions than the evaluated acoustic-probe and concept-readout baselines. Discussion These findings show that protocol-specific respiratory sound classification can be based on concept-associated latent evidence while retaining a constrained route for information outside the predefined concept set. However, Evi-CARD is not a strict scalar concept bottleneck, and no clinical meaning is assigned to its residual-memory slots. The evidence is limited to within-cohort cross-validation; independent-cohort testing, device- and site-stratified evaluation, and clinician review remain necessary before considering clinical deployment.

As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes integrated into academic writing, understanding how second language (L2) English students revise AI-assisted writing remains underexplored; therefore, this inductive content analysis explores students’ revision strategies for academic writing to propose a conceptual framework . The study employs an open-ended free listing task with 100 students, who listed their five major strategies for revising AI-assisted writing assignments. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 students experienced in revising AI-assisted writing. The interview transcripts were open-coded to develop categories. Meanwhile, the free-listing responses were directly categorized because participants listed strategies as explicit codes. The researcher then compared, consolidated, and synthesized the strategy categories into broader themes to form a conceptual framework. The analysis found key revision strategies like incorporating personal ideas and expressions, simplifying the language, consulting additional sources, paraphrasing and rewriting content, integrating personal experience, contextualizing AI content, and cross-checking AI information. It suggested that L2 English students primarily personalize and improve AI-assisted writing rather than passively accepting AI-generated text, while also adapting, evaluating, and responsibly managing AI-generated content. This final synthesis yielded six overarching themes: supportive utilization, ethical engagement, creative reform, critical evaluation, contextual revision, and functional adjustment. The proposed framework with six themes serves as an empirically grounded taxonomy of student revision strategies in AI-assisted writing.

Game development is a form of software development, but one whose constraints have no clean counterpart elsewhere: requirements that are discovered by playing rather than specified up front, teams in which programmers are a minority among artists and designers, and a notion of ''correct'' that ultimately reduces to whether the game is fun. The Foundations of Applied Software Engineering for Games workshop (FaSE4Games) exists to bring software-engineering methods to bear on those constraints, and to bring the resulting evidence back to the software-engineering community. The 2026 edition was co-located with the ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2026) in Montreal, Canada, and held as a half-day event on July 6th, 2026. It featured one keynote, four paper presentations, and a peak of 21 participants. The contributions ranged from mining game repositories for issue-resolution patterns and multiagent reinforcement learning for automated game testing, to large language models as a source of runtime content, and agile practice in student game-design teams. This report summarises the keynote, the presented papers, the discussions they prompted, and our reflections on the edition.

Software vulnerabilities can cause severe operational and financial damage to individuals and organizations in the event of cyber attacks. For example, the Log4J vulnerability can make millions of systems worldwide open to cyber attacks and potentially cause billions of dollars of damage. Software Vulnerability Management (SVM) is a critical process during software development to ensure software security and prevent these dangerous cyber attacks. SVM typically contains various phases such as detection, assessment, prioritization, fixing/patching, and reporting/disclosure. In the last 10 years, there has been an unprecedented rise in the size and complexity of software systems. For instance, the codebase of Google services contains more than two billion lines of code. This in turn requires new technologies, tools, and practices for SVM to ensure the security of such systems. The 4th International Workshop on Software Vulnerability Management (SVM 2026), co-located with ICSE 2026 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, provided a venue that brought together academics, industry, and government practitioners to present and discuss the state-of-the-art and state-of-the-practice of SVM to support both current and emerging software technologies and infrastructures. The workshop featured one invited talk and six paper presentations covering vulnerability management for cyber-physical systems, enhancements to static analysis for vulnerability detection and cryptographic API misuse, the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for secure coding and vulnerability analysis, as well as human factors in the reintroduction of vulnerabilities.

Curriculum learning orders samples by difficulty, but difficulty alone does not establish supervision reliability for dense prediction. Easy samples can expose shortcuts, hard samples can be informative, and noisy or ambiguous samples can mislead training. Building on our conference method CurriSeg, we present PaceShift, a stabilize-then-challenge paradigm combining supervision-adaptive curriculum selection with guarded spectral post-training. A learning-dynamics view motivates separating supervision reliability from temporal update value and applying spectral challenges after stabilization. The first phase estimates reliability from available supervision, augmentation consistency, model disagreement, and prediction certainty. Temporal statistics guide sample weighting, while pixel-uncertainty weights reduce the early influence of uncertain regions. The second phase ranks predictions from multiple spectral views using supervision agreement, robustness, reference consistency, and penalties. A pairwise preference objective measured against the frozen Phase-I reference, together with an anchor, refines the prediction. The framework supports full, weak, semi-supervised, and model-derived supervision. Experiments across context-entangled content segmentation (CECS), broader dense-prediction tasks, and foundation-model and cross-modal adaptations show accuracy gains. Targeted diagnostics indicate improved pooled calibration and corruption robustness in the evaluated settings. PaceShift preserves the deployed architecture and adds no inference computation. Code will be publicly released.
